title: Did Aesop really exist?
subtitle: The slave who told the truth
subject: litterature
description: A slave, ugly, mute from birth: the legend of Aesop is too good to be true. Behind it lies an invention that has outlived the centuries, the fable.
author: simon-lea

hero.hook: More fables are credited to him than one man could write in a lifetime, and nobody knows whether he ever lived.

blocks.text: Legend makes [[Aesop]] a Greek slave who lived around **600 to 500** BC, the father of the [[fable]]. The historian Herodotus, the comic playwright Aristophanes and the philosopher Plato all mention him. Yet the first known collection of his fables, put together by [[Demetrius of Phalerum]] in the **4th century** BC, appeared long after his death. If, that is, he was ever alive.

Nobody knows for sure whether a man called Aesop really existed. The best way to think of him is as a half-historical figure, like **Robin Hood**: a real storyteller, and then a legend that added a good deal of fiction to the facts. One thing is certain: far more fables are attributed to him than one man could have written.

Our popular image of Aesop comes from a collection of fables put together by a Roman slave, [[Phaedrus]], in the **1st or 2nd century** AD. There, Aesop is a very ugly slave, born mute, to whom the goddess [[Isis]] gives eloquent speech. A cunning man, he constantly outsmarts his master, a philosopher. In the end he quarrels with the god Apollo and is hurled off a cliff. The real Aesop, if there was one, may have ended that way.

blocks.caption: Aesop as seen by Velázquez around 1638, a book in his hand (Prado Museum).

blocks.text: Ugly and a slave: in Greek society, Aesop is the lowest of the low. And yet, through his fables, he is the one who speaks the truth, and he speaks it to people far more powerful than himself. He embodies the archetype of the trickster, the cunning, powerless character who dares to speak frankly to the powerful.

A fable can be defined as **a fiction picturing truth**. Every word counts. First, a fable must be invented. With real people and actual events, it would no longer work: readers would think only about the reality behind the tale. And since fables speak truth to power, naming real individuals and institutions would be very dangerous.

blocks.caption: "The Hare and the Tortoise" by Arthur Rackham, 1912: the tortoise plods on while the hare sleeps.

blocks.text: Second, a fable brings ideas to life through vivid, imaginary imagery. In Aesop, it is always talking animals or personified forces of nature. These symbols remain open to interpretation: his readers often note that the same fable can be read in conflicting ways. Finally, a fable expresses a truth. In *The Hare and the Tortoise*, it is that slow and steady wins the race.
The moral of an Aesop fable is often spelled out in black and white. Placed before the story, it is called a promythium; placed after it, an epimythium.

Deceptively simple, with an easy lesson to remember, fables seem made for children. For the most part, they are. Some, however, are considered too violent or too ambiguous for the very young. For a long time they were also used to teach schoolchildren **Latin**. But for hundreds of years, Aesop's fables were meant primarily for adults.

When they were being created, fables often served as a tool for the most marginalized, a way to share what they had learned about surviving in ruthlessly hierarchical societies. It is no accident that Aesop was a slave, as Phaedrus was after him. The early morals often taught slaves how to deal with their masters, hidden behind tales of wolves and foxes, sheep and lambs.

sections.title: Fables all the way to Orwell

blocks.text: Aesop's fables are still read today, mostly to children. But their morals have become part of common sense the world over. Like proverbs, they are invoked in a few words to help us navigate life. Things are not always as they seem: that is *The Wolf in Sheep's Clothing*. Necessity is the mother of invention: that is *The Crow and the Pitcher*.

The writing of fables did not end with antiquity. *Animal Farm*, which [[George Orwell]] published in **1945**, is a lengthy fable: personified animals and a moral, absolute power corrupts. It also contains often-quoted lines that speak truth to power.

blocks.caption: A pig in a suit and tie: the personified animal of Orwell's fable, on a mural.

blocks.text: All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.

The audience has changed, but the trick remains: talking beasts telling people what they would rather not hear. Aesop himself remains out of reach, between history and legend, as if the inventor of the fable were a fable himself.
Whether or not Aesop existed, the fable attributed to him, a fiction picturing truth, has let the powerless speak truth to power since antiquity.
